lead: This unit explains how a reinforced concrete beam carries shear and torsion, and how steel and concrete stick together. You will learn to compute shear stress, design stirrups, handle torsion, check combined actions, and fix development length, laps and detailing. After it you can take a beam section and produce a safe, buildable reinforcement layout.
about: The unit starts with 3.1, the behaviour of RC beams in shear: diagonal cracking and the truss idea. 3.2 turns that demand into stirrup spacing and checks. 3.3 adds torsion, converting torque into equivalent shear and moment. 3.4, taught by only a few universities, combines bending, shear and torsion. 3.5 explains bond and development length, the base for 3.6 lap splices and curtailment, also advanced. 3.7 collects code detailing rules. Earlier units supply flexural design and material factors; later units use these rules for slabs, columns and footings.

chapters.idea: Shear in an RC beam is diagonal tension: cracks form where principal tensile stress exceeds concrete strength, and the beam resists through concrete, aggregate interlock, dowel action and stirrups.
chapters.depth: Cover modes of shear failure: diagonal tension, shear-compression and web crushing. Define the critical section at distance d from the support face, nominal shear stress τ_v = V_u/(b_w d), where V_u is factored shear, b_w is web width and d is effective depth. Give design shear strength of concrete τ_c from IS 456 tables, maximum shear stress τ_c,max, and the effect of percentage tension steel. Show the truss analogy and why stirrups are vertical or inclined. Some syllabi call this 'behaviour of RC beams in shear' or 'modes of failure in shear'.

figure.aria: A shear load opens a diagonal crack; the beam then carries it by concrete compression, aggregate interlock, dowel action and stirrups.

chapters.example: A rectangular beam has b = 300 mm, overall depth D = 600 mm, effective depth d = 550 mm. The factored shear at the critical section is V_u = 180 kN. Concrete is M25 with τ_c = 0.62 MPa and τ_c,max = 3.1 MPa. Find τ_v. Answer: τ_v = 180×10³/(300×550) = 1.09 MPa. Since 0.62 < 1.09 < 3.1 MPa, concrete alone is not enough and shear reinforcement is needed.
chapters.trap: Using the maximum shear at the support instead of V_u at the critical section d away; or forgetting that τ_c depends on percentage tension steel and concrete grade.
chapters.prereq: Unit 1 for limit state factors and material strengths; Unit 2 for singly reinforced beam section and effective depth.
chapters.leave: Stirrup spacing design to 3.2; torsion to 3.3-3.4; flexural steel design to Unit 2.

chapters.idea: Shear reinforcement carries the shear that concrete cannot, using vertical stirrups or bent-up bars, with spacing chosen from V_us = 0.87 f_y A_sv d / s_v.
chapters.depth: Give design steps: compute V_u and τ_v; check τ_v ≤ τ_c,max; find V_uc = τ_c b_w d; if V_u > V_uc compute V_us = V_u − V_uc. Choose two-legged or four-legged stirrups, A_sv = area of stirrup legs, and spacing s_v. Apply minimum shear reinforcement and maximum spacing limits, commonly 0.75d or 300 mm, with tighter rules near curtailment. Include bent-up bars as an alternative and the code checks. Some syllabi call it 'design for shear' and 'design shear strength with and without shear reinforcement'.

figure.aria: The design flow takes factored shear to nominal stress, subtracts concrete capacity, and ends with 8 mm stirrups at 250 mm spacing.

chapters.example: Design vertical stirrups for a beam b = 300 mm, d = 550 mm, V_u = 180 kN, M25 concrete with τ_c = 0.62 MPa and τ_c,max = 3.1 MPa. Use Fe415 steel and two-legged 8 mm stirrups. Answer: τ_v = 1.09 MPa; V_uc = 0.62×300×550/1000 = 102.3 kN; V_us = 77.7 kN; A_sv = 2×50.3 = 100.6 mm²; s_v = 0.87×415×100.6×550/(77.7×10³) = 257 mm, use 250 mm; maximum spacing = min(0.75×550, 300) = 300 mm, so 250 mm is safe.
chapters.trap: Forgetting the minimum shear reinforcement when V_us is small or zero; using τ_v > τ_c,max as the only check; mixing N and kN in the spacing formula.
chapters.prereq: Chapter 3.1 for τ_v and τ_c; Unit 2 for beam section and effective depth.
chapters.leave: Torsion shear to 3.3; anchorage of stirrups to 3.5; detailing to 3.7.

chapters.idea: Torsion in a beam adds shear stresses around the section; IS 456 converts torque T_u into an equivalent shear V_e and equivalent moment M_t so the beam can be designed with ordinary shear and flexural steel.
chapters.depth: Distinguish equilibrium torsion, needed for stability, from compatibility torsion, where redistribution is allowed. Define torsional moment T_u. Compute equivalent shear V_e = V_u + 1.6 T_u/b and equivalent moment M_t = T_u(1 + D/b)/1.7, with b and D in the same units. Design transverse reinforcement for V_e and longitudinal steel for M_t plus bending. Check τ_ve ≤ τ_c,max; use closed stirrups and corner bars. Some syllabi call it 'design strength in torsion' or 'modes of failure in torsion'.

figure.aria: A torque of 30 kN·m becomes an equivalent shear of 280 kN and moment of 52.9 kN·m, which are carried by closed stirrups and longitudinal bars.

chapters.example: A beam has b = 300 mm, D = 600 mm, V_u = 120 kN and T_u = 30 kN·m at a section. Find V_e and M_t. Answer: V_e = 120 + 1.6×30/0.3 = 280 kN; M_t = 30×(1 + 600/300)/1.7 = 52.9 kN·m. Longitudinal steel is designed for M_u + 52.9 kN·m; stirrups are designed for 280 kN.
chapters.trap: Using T_u in kN·m with b in mm without converting units; or treating compatibility torsion as full equilibrium torsion.
chapters.prereq: Chapters 3.1-3.2 for shear stress and stirrup design; Unit 2 for flexural steel.
chapters.leave: Combined interaction to 3.4; anchorage of torsion bars to 3.5.

chapters.idea: When bending, shear and torsion act together, the section is designed for an equivalent moment M + M_t and equivalent shear V_e; the longitudinal and transverse steels must both be checked.
chapters.depth: Only a few universities teach this as a separate chapter. Cover the IS 456 route: compute M_t and V_e from T_u; design longitudinal steel for M_u + M_t; design stirrups for V_e; check τ_ve = V_e/(b d) ≤ τ_c,max; ensure side-face and corner bars. Explain that interaction is not a simple sum but the code's equivalent load method. Some syllabi phrase it 'design for combined bending, shear and torsion'.

figure.aria: Bending M, shear V and torsion T combine: T becomes M_t and V_e, and the final design uses M + M_t and V_e.

chapters.example: A beam section has b = 300 mm, D = 600 mm, d = 550 mm, factored M_u = 150 kN·m, V_u = 120 kN and T_u = 30 kN·m. Find the design moment and equivalent shear. Answer: M_t = 30×(1 + 600/300)/1.7 = 52.9 kN·m; design moment = 150 + 52.9 = 202.9 kN·m; V_e = 120 + 1.6×30/0.3 = 280 kN; τ_ve = 280×10³/(300×550) = 1.70 MPa. Check against τ_c,max before detailing.
chapters.trap: Adding M_u and M_t without checking units; forgetting to design stirrups for V_e rather than only V_u.
chapters.prereq: Chapter 3.3 for M_t and V_e; Chapter 3.2 for stirrup design; Unit 2 for flexural design.
chapters.leave: Serviceability deflection and crack width to Unit 2; full detailing to 3.7.

chapters.idea: Bond is the shear transfer between steel and concrete; development length L_d is the embedment needed to develop the bar force without pull-out.
chapters.depth: Cover flexural bond and anchorage bond, bond stress τ_bd, and IS 456 development length L_d = φ σ_s/(4 τ_bd), with σ_s = 0.87 f_y for tension. Use τ_bd from code tables for concrete grade and bar type. Explain anchorage at supports, end hooks, and why deformed bars need shorter L_d than plain bars. Include the check at simple supports and at points of bar curtailment. Some syllabi call this 'bond failure and strength'.

figure.aria: Development length rises linearly with bar diameter; the point for a 16 mm bar is 1031 mm.

chapters.example: Find the development length of a 16 mm Fe415 deformed bar in M25 concrete in tension. Take τ_bd = 1.4 MPa and σ_s = 0.87 f_y. Answer: σ_s = 0.87×415 = 361 MPa; L_d = 16×361/(4×1.4) = 1031 mm ≈ 1.03 m. Check that this length is available beyond the critical section.
chapters.trap: Using f_y instead of 0.87 f_y; using the bond stress for plain bars with deformed bars; forgetting that L_d must be available on the correct side of the critical section.
chapters.prereq: Chapters 3.1-3.2 for shear at supports; Unit 1 for partial safety factors; Unit 2 for bar stress.
chapters.leave: Lap splices and curtailment to 3.6; detailing rules to 3.7.

chapters.idea: A lap splice transfers force from one bar to another over a lap length, while curtailment stops bars where the bending moment has fallen, but only after development length and code rules are met.
chapters.depth: Only a few universities teach this as a separate chapter. Cover tension and compression laps, lap length not less than L_d and code minimum such as 30φ in flexural tension, staggering of laps, and curtailment of bars using the bending moment envelope. Show why bars are curtailed in steps and why development length must extend beyond the theoretical cut-off. Some syllabi call it 'splicing of reinforcement'.

figure.aria: Two bottom bars run full length; two are curtailed from 1.5 m to 4.5 m in a 6 m beam.

chapters.example: A simply supported beam of span 6 m has four 16 mm bars at midspan. Two bars are curtailed at 1.5 m from each support, leaving a 3 m central length. For a 16 mm bar, L_d = 1.03 m. Check a lap of 1.2 m if the code minimum in flexural tension is 30φ. Answer: 30φ = 480 mm; required lap = max(1030, 480) = 1030 mm; 1.2 m is adequate. At the curtailment, the bar must extend L_d = 1.03 m beyond the theoretical cut-off.
chapters.trap: Curtailing bars exactly at the theoretical point of zero moment; forgetting that the cut-off point must be shifted by L_d; using a lap shorter than L_d.
chapters.prereq: Chapter 3.5 for L_d; Unit 2 for bending moment envelope.
chapters.leave: General detailing and drawings to 3.7; column splices to Unit 5.

chapters.idea: Detailing turns the calculated steel into a buildable drawing that satisfies cover, spacing, anchorage, lap and curtailment rules.
chapters.depth: Cover nominal and clear cover; minimum clear spacing between bars; stirrup spacing near supports and at curtailment; hooks and bend radii; development length and lap splices shown on the drawing; bar bending schedule basics. Use IS 456 detailing clauses and common site practice. Some syllabi call this 'detailing requirements'. Keep the chapter practical: every calculated bar must appear with a length and a position.

figure.aria: From outside inward, a beam section has 25 mm cover, an 8 mm stirrup, a 16 mm main bar, and 56.7 mm clear spacing between bars.

chapters.example: A beam is 300 mm wide with four 16 mm bars in one layer, 8 mm stirrups and 25 mm clear cover. Check the clear spacing between bars. Answer: width available inside stirrups = 300 − 2×25 − 2×8 = 234 mm; steel width = 4×16 = 64 mm; clear spacing = (234 − 64)/3 = 56.7 mm. This is greater than the minimum of max(16 mm, 25 mm) = 25 mm, so the layout is valid.
chapters.trap: Using nominal cover as clear cover; forgetting to subtract stirrup diameter when finding bar spacing; showing a lap without its length on the drawing.
chapters.prereq: Chapters 3.2, 3.3, 3.5 and 3.6 for stirrups, torsion bars, L_d and laps.
chapters.leave: Slab, column and footing detailing to Units 4 and 5; bar bending schedule software outside this unit.
